title: What makes a vector space
objectives: Check the vector space axioms for lists, polynomials and functions.

screens.title: Two fully invested portfolios
screens.prose: A portfolio of two funds is a weight vector. $\mathbf{u} = (0.6, 0.4)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (0.3, 0.7)$ are both fully invested: each one's weights total 1. Both sit on the dashed line $x + y = 1$.
screens.question: Add them. What is $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$?

hints.text: Add entry by entry.
First entries: $0.6 + 0.3$. Second entries: $0.4 + 0.7$.
$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = (0.9, 1.1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the first entries, then the second entries.

byKey.avg: You averaged the two portfolios. The sum adds the entries without halving.
byKey.one: You forced the total back to 1. The second entry is $0.4 + 0.7 = 1.1$.
byKey.length: Your answer has the wrong number of entries. It needs 2, one per coordinate.

explain.text: $0.6 + 0.3 = 0.9$ and $0.4 + 0.7 = 1.1$. The total weight is $1 + 1 = 2$, so the sum leaves the dashed line. Holdings in shares behave better: shares plus shares are shares.

screens.title: Can the sum stay on the line?
screens.prose: Drag both heads to other points of the dashed line. The caption shows each total weight. Try to put the sum on the line too.

derive.caption: Totals: $\mathbf{u}$ {{fixed(u.v[0] + u.v[1], 2)}}, $\mathbf{v}$ {{fixed(v.v[0] + v.v[1], 2)}}, $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$ {{fixed(u.v[0] + u.v[1] + v.v[0] + v.v[1], 2)}}

screens.question: When both totals are 1, what is the total of $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$?

options.text: 1, if we pick the weights well
options.why: You hoped some choice would work. The totals add: $1 + 1 = 2$ whatever the weights.

options.text: It depends on the angle between them
options.why: You looked at directions. The total of the sum is the sum of the totals.

hints.text: Watch the third number in the caption as you drag.
Each total is 1 while its head is on the line.
The sum's total is $1 + 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. Totals add, so the sum's total is always 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption with both heads on the line.

explain.text: The total of $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$ is the total of $\mathbf{u}$ plus the total of $\mathbf{v}$. On the line that is $1 + 1 = 2$. So adding never stays inside the set of fully invested portfolios.

screens.title: A vector space
screens.prose: A **vector space** over $\mathbb{F}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) is a set $V$ with two operations. Addition maps $V \times V \to V$ and scalar multiplication maps $\mathbb{F} \times V \to V$. The table lists the eight conditions, for all vectors and scalars (Axler 1.20).
screens.question: The fully invested weights fail before we reach the table. Why?

options.text: Their sum leaves the set, so addition is not a map into $V$.

options.why: You picked a condition that holds: $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}$ for any weights.
Short weights are allowed here. The trouble is the total, not the signs.

options.text: They do not fail: they lie on a line.
options.why: You trusted the picture. The line misses $(0, 0)$, and sums leave it.

hints.text: Both operations must land back in $V$.
We just added two of them and left the line.
Addition does not map $V \times V$ into $V$.

feedback.correct: Right. Addition must land in $V$, and here it does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the sum of two of them is still one of them.

explain.text: Each operation is a function into $V$, so sums and multiples must stay in $V$. Here $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$ has total 2. The eight conditions only make sense once that holds.

screens.title: Degree at most 2, or exactly 2
screens.prose: $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is the polynomials of degree at most 2, with the zero polynomial. The curves show $(x^2 + x) + (-x^2 + 1) = x + 1$. Compare it with the set of polynomials of degree **exactly** 2.
screens.question: Fill in yes or no for each set.

rows: Scalar multiples stay in the set
Every element has an additive inverse

hints.text: The sum on the canvas has degree 1.
$0 \cdot (x^2 + x)$ is the zero polynomial, and $-(x^2 + x)$ has degree 2.
$\mathcal{P}_2$: yes four times. Exactly 2: no, no, no, then yes.

feedback.correct: Right. Degree exactly 2 fails three checks, yet inverses exist.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each check on $x^2 + x$ and $-x^2 + 1$.

byKey.r0c2: You said sums stay. Here two degree-2 polynomials add to $x + 1$, of degree 1.
byKey.r1c2: You said multiples stay. Scaling by 0 gives the zero polynomial, which has no degree 2.
byKey.r2c2: The zero polynomial is the only candidate, and it is not of degree 2.
byKey.r3c2: $-(x^2 + x) = -x^2 - x$ has degree exactly 2, so inverses do exist.

explain.text: The $x^2$ terms cancel, so the sum drops to degree 1. The zero polynomial is missing too. $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ keeps the lower degrees, so it passes every check.

screens.title: Functions are vectors
screens.prose: $\mathbb{R}^{[0,1]}$ is the set of all functions from $[0, 1]$ to $\mathbb{R}$. We add them pointwise, $(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$, and scale them pointwise. A year of daily P&L is a function on $\{1, \dots, 252\}$: a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{252}$.
screens.question: What is $(f + g)(0.5)$?

hints.text: Pointwise means: evaluate each function at 0.5, then add.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $f(0.5)$ and $g(0.5)$, then add.

byKey.prod: You multiplied the values. The sum of functions adds them.

explain.text: $(f + g)(0.5) = 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75$, the green curve at the line. Each condition holds pointwise because it holds in $\mathbb{R}$. The zero vector is the function that is 0 everywhere.

screens.title: An odd scalar rule
screens.prose: Take $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the usual addition, but scale by $\lambda(a, b) = (\lambda a, 0)$. The picture shows $\mathbf{v} = (2, 3)$ and $1\mathbf{v}$ under this rule.
screens.question: Which condition fails?

options.why: Check it: both sides are $((\lambda + \mu)a, 0)$. It holds.
Check it: both sides have first entry $\lambda$ times the sum of first entries, and second entry 0.
Check it: both sides are $(\lambda\mu a, 0)$. It holds.

hints.text: Try each condition on $\mathbf{v} = (2, 3)$.
Look at the two arrows: is $1\mathbf{v}$ the same as $\mathbf{v}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each condition on $(2, 3)$.

explain.text: Under this rule $1(2, 3) = (2, 0)$, so the second entry is lost. The other scaling conditions survive, because both sides lose it alike. One failed condition is enough: this is not a vector space.

screens.title: It is a line, so it is a space
screens.prose: A classmate says the fully invested portfolios $\{(x, y) : x + y = 1\}$ form a vector space. Their reason: the points form a straight line, like the axes do.
screens.question: Which conditions does the dashed line fail? Select all that apply.

options.why: You ticked commutativity. It holds for any two vectors of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

options.text: None, since it is a straight line
options.why: You trusted the shape. A line that misses the origin is not a vector space.

hints.text: Is $(0, 0)$ on the line $x + y = 1$?
$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$ has total 2, and $-\mathbf{u}$ has total $-1$.
Zero, sums and multiples all fail. Commutativity holds.

feedback.correct: Right. It misses $\mathbf{0}$, and sums and multiples leave it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test $(0, 0)$, a sum and a multiple against $x + y = 1$.

byKey.comm: You ticked commutativity. Adding in either order gives the same vector, on or off the line.
byKey.nothing: You trusted the straight shape. The line misses $(0, 0)$, so it has no zero vector.

explain.text: $0 + 0 \ne 1$, so the origin is off the line. Sums have total 2 and $-\mathbf{u}$ has total $-1$. Only lines through the origin can be vector spaces.

screens.title: A strange space
screens.prose: Let $V$ be the positive reals. Define $x \oplus y = xy$ and $\lambda \odot x = x^{\lambda}$. All eight conditions hold: $(xy)^{\lambda} = x^{\lambda}y^{\lambda}$ is one distributive law. The zero vector must satisfy $x \oplus \mathbf{0} = x$ for every $x$.
screens.question: Which positive real is the zero vector?

hints.text: Here "adding" means multiplying.
Solve $x \cdot z = x$ for $z$.
$z = 1$, since $x \cdot 1 = x$.

feedback.correct: Right. $x \oplus 1 = x \cdot 1 = x$, so 1 is the zero vector.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $z$ with $x \oplus z = xz = x$ for all $x$.

byKey.zero: You took the usual zero. 0 is not a positive real, and $x \oplus 0 = 0$, not $x$.

explain.text: The zero vector is whatever adds as nothing. Here adding is multiplying, so it is 1. The smallest space of all is $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, where $\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$ and $\lambda\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$.

screens.title: Only one zero
screens.prose: From now on we prove facts from the eight conditions alone. First claim: a vector space has only one additive identity.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $\mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{0}'$ are both additive identities of $V$.
$\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0}' = \mathbf{0}' + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}'$, by commutativity and because $\mathbf{0}$ is an additive identity. So $\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}'$. $\blacksquare$
Both are $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$, so they are equal.
lines.why: You assumed $V$ is $\mathbb{F}^n$. $V$ may hold polynomials, functions or positive reals.

hints.text: Start by naming two additive identities.
Add them together: $\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0}'$.
Suppose two; the sum equals $\mathbf{0}$; the sum also equals $\mathbf{0}'$.

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0}'$ equals both, so they are equal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name two identities, then work out $\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0}'$ two ways.

byKey.d1: You kept the line about $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$. In the positive reals the zero is 1, so lists are not enough.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: $\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0}'$ is $\mathbf{0}$, because $\mathbf{0}'$ adds as nothing. It is also $\mathbf{0}'$, because $\mathbf{0}$ adds as nothing. One vector cannot be two, so the zero is unique.

screens.title: Zero times a vector
screens.prose: Claim: $0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for every $\mathbf{v} \in V$. On the left, $0$ is the scalar in $\mathbb{F}$. On the right, $\mathbf{0}$ is the zero vector of $V$. Nothing in the eight conditions says this directly.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Add the additive inverse $-(0\mathbf{v})$ to both sides.
The left side becomes $\mathbf{0}$. The right becomes $0\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{0} = 0\mathbf{v}$, by associativity and the identity. So $0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. $\blacksquare$
$0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, because zero times anything is zero.
lines.why: You assumed the claim. In $V$ we may only use the eight conditions.

hints.text: Split the scalar 0 as $0 + 0$.
That gives $0\mathbf{v} = 0\mathbf{v} + 0\mathbf{v}$.
Split; expand; add $-(0\mathbf{v})$; simplify.

feedback.correct: Right. Split 0 as $0 + 0$, expand, then cancel one $0\mathbf{v}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with $0 = 0 + 0$ in $\mathbb{F}$.

byKey.d1: You kept "zero times anything is zero". That is what we are proving, so it cannot be a step.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: We wrote $0\mathbf{v}$ as $0\mathbf{v} + 0\mathbf{v}$. Adding the inverse of $0\mathbf{v}$ cancels one copy. What is left says $\mathbf{0} = 0\mathbf{v}$.

screens.title: The reason for line 2
screens.prose: Line 2 of the proof says $(0 + 0)\mathbf{v} = 0\mathbf{v} + 0\mathbf{v}$. A stranger checking the proof asks which condition allows it.
screens.question: Which justifies line 2?

options.why: You picked commutativity. Line 2 swaps nothing; it expands a sum of scalars.
That fact justifies line 1, about scalars. Line 2 splits a vector into two vectors.

hints.text: Line 2 turns a sum of scalars times $\mathbf{v}$ into a sum of vectors.
Look for a condition with $(\lambda + \mu)\mathbf{v}$ on one side.
Take $\lambda = \mu = 0$ in $(\lambda + \mu)\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} + \mu\mathbf{v}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the condition that expands $(\lambda + \mu)\mathbf{v}$.

explain.text: $(\lambda + \mu)\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} + \mu\mathbf{v}$ with $\lambda = \mu = 0$ gives line 2. Line 1 used $0 + 0 = 0$, a fact about scalars. Mixing the two up confuses scalars with vectors.

screens.title: Which quant sets are spaces?
screens.prose: Each set uses the natural addition and scaling: entry by entry, or pointwise for functions. Run the checks on each.

rows: Holdings in shares (short and fractional allowed)
Daily P&L series over a year
Option payoffs as functions of the final price $S$

screens.question: Which are vector spaces over $\mathbb{R}$? Select all that apply.

options.why: You ticked long-only. $-1$ times a long portfolio is short, so scaling leaves the set.
You ticked fully invested. Two of them add to total weight 2.

hints.text: For each set, try $-1$ times an element, and a sum of two.
Long-only fails under $-1$; fully invested fails under $+$.
The first four are spaces; the last two are not.

feedback.correct: Right. Four are spaces; long-only and fully invested are not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test a sum and $-1$ times an element of each set.

byKey.long: You ticked long-only. Scaling by $-1$ turns it into a short portfolio, outside the set.
byKey.fully: You ticked fully invested. A sum of two has weights totalling 2.

explain.text: Holdings and P&L are lists, so they live in some $\mathbb{R}^n$. Demeaned series have mean 0, which survives sums and multiples. Payoffs are functions of $S$, added pointwise.

ideas: A vector space is a set with an addition and a scalar multiplication into it, meeting eight conditions.
Lists $\mathbb{F}^n$, polynomials $\mathcal{P}_m(\mathbb{F})$ and functions $\mathbb{R}^{S}$ are vector spaces. A set that loses sums, multiples or $\mathbf{0}$ is not.
From the conditions alone: the zero is unique, $0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, and $(-1)\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}$.

formula.name: Zero times a vector
formula.note: The middle step is distributivity over scalars.

summary.trap: A straight line is a vector space only if it passes through $\mathbf{0}$. The fully invested line $x + y = 1$ does not.

quiz.prose: Claim: $(-1)\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}$ for every $\mathbf{v} \in V$. Here $-\mathbf{v}$ is the additive inverse of $\mathbf{v}$.
quiz.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: So $(-1)\mathbf{v}$ is an additive inverse of $\mathbf{v}$. Inverses are unique, as zeros are, so $(-1)\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}$. $\blacksquare$
$(-1)\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}$, since $-1$ times a number is its negative.
lines.why: You used a fact about numbers. $\mathbf{v}$ may be a function or a positive real.

feedback.correct: Right. $(-1)\mathbf{v}$ adds to $\mathbf{v}$ to give $\mathbf{0}$, so it is the inverse.

byKey.d1: You used arithmetic of numbers. The proof may use only the eight conditions and what we proved.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Write $\mathbf{v}$ as $1\mathbf{v}$, combine the scalars and use $0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. So $(-1)\mathbf{v}$ undoes $\mathbf{v}$. Since a vector has only one inverse, it is $-\mathbf{v}$.

quiz.prose: In the positive reals with $x \oplus y = xy$ and $\lambda \odot x = x^{\lambda}$, the zero vector is 1.
quiz.question: What is the additive inverse of 2?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $w$ with $2 \oplus w = 2w = 1$.

byKey.neg: You took the usual negative. $-2$ is not a positive real, and $2 \oplus w$ means $2w$.
byKey.same: You gave 2 itself. $2 \oplus 2 = 4$, not the zero vector 1.

explain.text: The inverse $w$ must give $2 \oplus w = \mathbf{0}$, that is $2w = 1$. So $w = \tfrac12$. It is also $(-1) \odot 2 = 2^{-1}$, as the last proof predicts.

options.text: No: it is too small to hold a basis.
options.why: You asked for a basis. The definition asks only for the eight conditions.
It does: $\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{0}$ is its own inverse.

feedback.correct: Right. The zero space is a vector space.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each condition with the one vector there is.

explain.text: Every side of every condition is $\mathbf{0}$. So all eight hold, and both operations land in $V$. It is the smallest vector space.

quiz.prose: Two traders' daily P&L over a 252-day year are $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$. The desk's P&L is $\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}$, day by day.
quiz.question: Which space holds $\mathbf{p}$, $\mathbf{q}$ and $\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}$?

options.why: You summed over the days. Each P&L series keeps all 252 numbers.
You counted the traders. Each vector has one entry per day.
That holds functions on an interval. Trading days are a finite set.

feedback.correct: Right. One entry per trading day: $\mathbb{R}^{252}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the entries in one P&L series.

explain.text: A P&L series assigns a number to each day $1, \dots, 252$. That is a function on a 252-point set, the same as a list in $\mathbb{R}^{252}$. The desk's sum adds day by day.
